old: It is an island that floats, as it were, upon the sea
new: It is an island that floats (as it were) upon the sea
reason: Butler writes 'floats (as it were) upon the sea'; PUNCTUATION.md §6 says an aside that is a phrase keeps its parentheses, and this one was converted to commas unrecorded (continuity §5 says no mark of Butler's is changed).

old: in the end I judged it best
new: in the end I thought it best
reason: Butler's 'in the end I deemed it best' is the formula GLOSSARY fixes as 'thought it best' (accepted B05-P037 'In the end he thought it best', B06-P012); 'judged' gives the same Butler formula a second rendering.

old: a fathom or so of good stout rope
new: a fathom or so—about six feet—of good stout rope
reason: Butler's 'a fathom or so' is the edition's first fathom (none in Books 1–9); WORKFLOW's accessibility standard glosses an unfamiliar unit briefly at first use, on the pilot's model, and a listener cannot otherwise picture the rope's length.

old: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared,
new: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared,
reason: Butler's 'When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared' is the dawn formula GLOSSARY (Book 2 table) fixes as 'When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared' for every recurrence, as Books 3, 4, 5, 8 and 9 (B09-P009, P020, P032, P044) print it; Book 10 alone keeps Butler's order.

old: as though you were dumb
new: as though you were mute
reason: Butler's 'as though you were dumb' means speechless, but a present-day listener most readily hears 'dumb' as 'stupid', which would turn Circe's concern into an insult.

old: woollen cloaks
new: woolen cloaks
reason: Butler's British 'woollen'; the spelling standard (GLOSSARY) makes it 'woolen', as accepted B01, B04 and B07 print it. Pilot chapter finding C2, still present.

old: for a whole twelvemonth
new: for a whole year
reason: Butler's 'a whole twelvemonth'; GLOSSARY lists 'twelvemonth' by name among the dead forms the archaism guard must catch, and accepted Books 1, 2 and 4 render it 'twelve months' (continuity §6's claim that it is current contradicts the glossary).

old: in the covered cloisters
new: in the covered gallery
reason: Butler's 'covered cloisters'; GLOSSARY fixes 'cloisters' as 'the gallery' (Book 1 row), and accepted B01-P026 and B04-P069 render the identical phrase 'the covered gallery'.

old: dig a trench a cubit or so in length, breadth, and depth
new: dig a trench a cubit or so—roughly eighteen inches—in length, breadth, and depth
reason: Butler's 'a cubit or so' is the edition's first cubit; WORKFLOW and GLOSSARY name the gloss 'cubit → roughly eighteen inches' as the model for first-use unit glosses, and the candidate omits it.

old: fastening it with a golden girdle round her waist
new: fastening it with a golden belt round her waist
reason: Butler's 'golden girdle round her waist'; GLOSSARY fixes 'girdle' → 'belt' and accepted B05-P020 renders the same goddess-dressing image 'a beautiful golden belt about her waist'.

old: they did as I asked them
new: they did as I told them
reason: Butler's 'they did as I bade them' is a command, which GLOSSARY renders with 'tell' ('do as I bid you' → 'as I tell you'); 'asked' softens Odysseus's order to the crew into a request.

old: iron-bound with a wall that girds it
new: with an iron-bound wall that encircles it
reason: "girds" is an uncommon, archaic verb for "wraps around/encircles"; a listener unfamiliar with the word has nothing in the sentence to fall back on.

old: to hold the ways of the roaring winds
new: to hold the paths of the roaring winds
reason: "ways" meaning "routes/courses" is an archaic sense; on first hearing it more naturally reads as "manners/habits," which doesn't fit and forces a re-parse.

old: he could rouse or still each one of them as he pleased
new: he could stir up or calm each one of them as he pleased
reason: "still" used as a verb ("calm") is easy to mis-hear as the adverb "still" (yet), producing a momentary garden-path misread when listened to rather than read.

old: So they talked, and evil counsels won the day.
new: So they talked, and the evil advice won out.
reason: "evil counsels won the day" is a period idiom personifying abstract "counsels"; a modern listener has to work to connect it to "they gave in to the bad idea." [lead: wording adjusted to stay close to Butler]

old: and this last answers the greeting
new: and the one leaving answers the greeting
reason: "this last" as a stand-in for "the latter" is a formal written construction, not spoken English, and is disorienting heard aloud without the option to reread.

old: a man who could do without sleep might earn double wages, one as a herdsman of cattle and another as a shepherd
new: a man who could do without sleep might earn double wages — one wage as a herdsman of cattle, another as a shepherd
reason: "one" and "another" immediately follow "a man," so a listener may briefly take them to mean two different men rather than two jobs held by the same man.

old: for the stag was much too big for me to carry on my shoulder, steadying him with one hand
new: for the stag was much too big for me to carry on my shoulder while steadying him with one hand
reason: "steadying him with one hand" is left dangling after "leaning on my spear," so the listener has to work backward to figure out which hand is doing what; the physical picture briefly falls apart. [lead: wording adjusted to stay close to Butler]

old: disguised as a young man in the first bloom of his youth and beauty, with the down just coming on his face
new: disguised as a young man in the first bloom of his youth and beauty, with the first soft beard just coming on his face
reason: "the down" (fine new facial hair) is a homograph with the common word "down" (direction); heard aloud, "the down just coming on his face" can momentarily misread before the meaning resolves. [lead: wording adjusted to stay close to Butler]

old: she will unman you and make you fit for nothing
new: she will strip you of your manhood and leave you helpless
reason: "unman" is a dated verb whose meaning (render impotent/powerless) isn't recoverable from sound alone for a listener who hasn't met the word before.

old: brought me water in a beautiful golden ewer
new: brought me water in a beautiful golden pitcher
reason: "ewer" is an archaic word for a water jug that most modern listeners won't recognize.

old: You will find it near the place where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus (which is a branch of the river Styx) flow into Acheron
new: You will find it near the place where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus — a branch of the river Styx — flow into the river Acheron
reason: Four unfamiliar proper nouns plus a parenthetical aside land in one sentence; very hard to track by ear even though the exact names aren't essential to following the instructions that follow (go to where the rivers meet).
